question: You have four hours to learn vocabulary for a test in two weeks. Which plan fits the research this lesson summarises?
options: Four one-hour sessions on different days
One four-hour session the night before
Any split works; only total hours count
why: Research on verbal recall generally favours spreading the same study time across sessions; total hours alone do not decide later recall.

claim.text: Research on verbal recall generally favours spreading the same study time across sessions; total hours alone do not decide later recall.

question: You want to check that you know the Spanish words on a two-column list. Which check makes you retrieve each word?
options: Read down both columns slowly, twice
Fold over the Spanish column, then say each word
Tick each Spanish word you recognise on sight
why: Hiding the answer removes the reading route, so you have to produce it; rereading and recognising still show it to you.

claim.text: Hiding the answer removes the reading route, so you have to produce it; rereading and recognising still show it to you.

question: A card asks 'Who signed the treaty, where and when?' and you get it half right. What change shows which part you missed?
options: Add more detail to the same card
Answer the same card faster next time
Split it into three cards, one fact each
why: With one target per cue, each miss points at one fact; a compound card hides which part failed.

claim.text: With one target per cue, each miss points at one fact; a compound card hides which part failed.

question: Your notes cover three rivers. Which flashcard cue has exactly one right answer?
why: A cue that names its context picks out one fact; 'Length?' could mean any of the three rivers.

claim.text: A cue that names its context picks out one fact; 'Length?' could mean any of the three rivers.

question: You can say 'dog' when you see 'perro'. Which check tests the other direction?
why: Swapping cue and answer tests the opposite mapping; success in one direction is not a test of the other.

claim.text: Swapping cue and answer tests the opposite mapping; success in one direction is not a test of the other.

question: You must remember the steps wash, rinse, dry. Which check tests their order, not just the words?
options: Pick the three step words out of a list of six
Write the three steps in sequence from memory
Say each step word once, in any order
why: Order is checked by comparing positions; recognising the right words says nothing about their sequence.

claim.text: Order is checked by comparing positions; recognising the right words says nothing about their sequence.

question: Your meeting note has three fields: room, day and code. How do you find a value you do not actually know?
options: Cover the values and fill each field from memory
Reread the note slowly until it feels familiar
Check that each of the three fields has a value
why: Reconstructing each value exposes the specific gap; a complete-looking note can still hide one you could not produce.

claim.text: Reconstructing each value exposes the specific gap; a complete-looking note can still hide one you could not produce.

question: Your notes say: alarm rings, then you wake, then you catch the bus. Which check tests the explanation, not just the words?
options: Count how many of the events you remember
Rebuild the chain from cause to result
why: The explanation is the ordered links; an alphabetical list or a count drops the cause-and-result order.

claim.text: The explanation is the ordered links; an alphabetical list or a count drops the cause-and-result order.

question: Apply the ascending rule to 12, 3 and 8. Which order is correct?
why: Ascending means smallest to largest: 3 < 8 < 12. Quoting the rule is not the same as applying it.

claim.text: Ascending means smallest to largest: 3 < 8 < 12. Quoting the rule is not the same as applying it.

question: Parts BX7 and BX8 are both described as 'mounting bracket'. Which note tells them apart?
options: BX7 steel bracket, BX8 steel bracket
BX7 left bracket, BX8 right bracket
Mounting bracket, part code BX7 or BX8
why: Confusable codes need a field that differs between them; a shared description fits both.

claim.text: Confusable codes need a field that differs between them; a shared description fits both.

question: You feel sure you know a four-step route. Which gives you evidence you can check?
options: Write the steps, then compare with notes
Rate your confidence out of ten
Skim it to see if it feels familiar
why: A written attempt can be compared step by step; a feeling of familiarity cannot be checked against anything.

claim.text: A written attempt can be compared step by step; a feeling of familiarity cannot be checked against anything.

question: You wrote a five-step sequence from memory. Which feedback tells you what to fix?
options: A note saying this was your third attempt
Your attempt beside the target, errors marked
A note saying 'not quite, try again'
why: Side-by-side comparison locates the wrong position; a count or a bare 'wrong' does not say which item.

claim.text: Side-by-side comparison locates the wrong position; a count or a bare 'wrong' does not say which item.

question: Your calendar is free 10:00–10:30, then a 10:30 meeting 25 minutes away (no delays). How much of that slot is really free?
why: The 25-minute trip occupies 10:05–10:30, so only five minutes remain before you leave.

claim.text: The 25-minute trip occupies 10:05–10:30, so only five minutes remain before you leave.

question: A call booked 9:00–9:30 may run up to ten minutes over. When should the next task start so an overrun cannot collide?
why: A gap absorbs delay up to its length; ten minutes of overrun needs a ten-minute gap, so 9:40.

claim.text: A gap absorbs delay up to its length; ten minutes of overrun needs a ten-minute gap, so 9:40.

question: A 45-minute report is due at 17:00. What is the latest start?
why: Latest start = deadline minus duration: 17:00 − 45 minutes = 16:15.

claim.text: Latest start = deadline minus duration: 17:00 − 45 minutes = 16:15.

question: A 15:00 pitch needs 40 minutes of preparation, and you are free from 14:00. Which booking works?
why: Preparation must finish before the event that depends on it, so it needs its own block ending by 15:00.

claim.text: Preparation must finish before the event that depends on it, so it needs its own block ending by 15:00.

question: A task takes 20 to 35 minutes. You start at 13:00 and have a fixed call at 13:30. What does checking the longer estimate show?
options: It fits with 10 minutes to spare
It may run 5 minutes into the call
why: At the upper end 13:00 + 35 minutes = 13:35, past the 13:30 call; the short estimate hides that.

claim.text: At the upper end 13:00 + 35 minutes = 13:35, past the 13:30 call; the short estimate hides that.

question: You put 'write report 10:00–11:00' and 'phone cover 10:30–11:00' on two calendar rows. Both are yours. How much time is double-booked?
options: None; they are on separate rows
why: One person runs one block at a time; 10:30–11:00 is booked twice whichever row it is drawn on.

claim.text: One person runs one block at a time; 10:30–11:00 is booked twice whichever row it is drawn on.

question: A fixed call runs 11:00–11:30. A movable 25-minute task must not overlap it and must be done before the call. What is its latest start?
why: The call cannot move, so the task must end by 11:00: 11:00 − 25 minutes = 10:35.

claim.text: The call cannot move, so the task must end by 11:00: 11:00 − 25 minutes = 10:35.

question: A client call runs 14:00–14:45 and needs 15 minutes of notes afterwards. When are you actually free?
why: The notes are required work too: 14:45 + 15 minutes = 15:00.

claim.text: The notes are required work too: 14:45 + 15 minutes = 15:00.

question: Your afternoon has free gaps of 20, 15 and 25 minutes. Does a 40-minute task that cannot be split fit?
options: No; the longest gap is 25 minutes
Yes, using the two largest gaps
why: An unsplittable task needs one continuous gap at least as long as it; 25 < 40, whatever the total.

claim.text: An unsplittable task needs one continuous gap at least as long as it; 25 < 40, whatever the total.

question: Ana drafts 9:00–10:30. Bo reviews for 30 minutes and cannot review a partial draft. When can the review end, at the earliest?
why: The review starts when the draft is released at 10:30, so it ends at 11:00 at the earliest.

claim.text: The review starts when the draft is released at 10:30, so it ends at 11:00 at the earliest.

question: A print job takes 20 minutes plus 10 minutes of printer setup. You have a 25-minute slot. Does it fit?
why: The booking is setup plus work: 10 + 20 = 30 minutes, more than the 25-minute slot.

claim.text: The booking is setup plus work: 10 + 20 = 30 minutes, more than the 25-minute slot.

question: You must arrive at 9:00. The trip takes 35 minutes with no delay. When must you leave, at the latest?
why: Departure = arrival minus trip: 9:00 − 35 minutes = 8:25.

claim.text: Departure = arrival minus trip: 9:00 − 35 minutes = 8:25.

question: Your 9:00–12:00 is fully booked. An urgent 15-minute request arrives. Where can it go without moving anything?
why: Slack is explicit free time; a fully booked morning has none, however long it is.

claim.text: Slack is explicit free time; a fully booked morning has none, however long it is.

question: Three people wait at one desk with jobs of 2, 8 and 20 minutes, all ready now. Which order gives the least total waiting?
why: Total waiting is the sum of start times: 0 + 2 + 10 = 12 for 2, 8, 20, against 0 + 20 + 28 = 48 for 20, 8, 2.

claim.text: Total waiting is the sum of start times: 0 + 2 + 10 = 12 for 2, 8, 20, against 0 + 20 + 28 = 48 for 20, 8, 2.

question: Job A takes 10 minutes and is due at minute 10. Job B takes 3 minutes and is due at minute 30. Which order misses no deadline?
why: A then B finishes A at 10 and B at 13, both on time; B first pushes A to minute 13, past its deadline.

claim.text: A then B finishes A at 10 and B at 13, both on time; B first pushes A to minute 13, past its deadline.

question: 'Send invoice' is top priority but needs a signed quote first. Which order is possible?
options: Send the invoice first; it is top priority
Get the quote, then send the invoice
Do both at the same moment
why: A priority label does not remove a prerequisite; the invoice cannot go before its input exists.

claim.text: A priority label does not remove a prerequisite; the invoice cannot go before its input exists.

question: Tasks: email, call, email, call. Each change between email and calls costs 2 minutes. Which order costs least switching?
why: Grouping needs one switch (2 minutes); alternating needs three (6 minutes).

claim.text: Grouping needs one switch (2 minutes); alternating needs three (6 minutes).

question: A colleague's 2-hour build cannot start until you send a 5-minute config. You also have 30 minutes of tidying. What first?
why: The short input releases the dependent build; doing the tidying first delays the build by 30 minutes.

claim.text: The short input releases the dependent build; doing the tidying first delays the build by 30 minutes.

question: Three 5-minute jobs and a 20-minute job due at minute 22 are all ready. If you do the short jobs first, when does the long job finish?
why: 5 + 5 + 5 + 20 = 35, past minute 22; starting the long job first would finish it at 20.

claim.text: 5 + 5 + 5 + 20 = 35, past minute 22; starting the long job first would finish it at 20.

question: Three 10-minute tasks. You either finish them one by one, or rotate 5 minutes on each. When is the first task done in each plan?
options: Minute 10 one by one; minute 20 rotating
Minute 10 one by one; minute 10 rotating
Minute 10 one by one; minute 5 rotating
why: Rotating, the first task gets its second 5 minutes at 15–20, so it completes at 20, not 10.

claim.text: Rotating, the first task gets its second 5 minutes at 15–20, so it completes at 20, not 10.

question: 'Print poster' is blocked until the logo arrives in an hour. 'Book the room' needs nothing. What can you do now?
options: Print the poster without the logo
why: Ready work has its inputs; the poster is blocked, but the room booking can run now.

claim.text: Ready work has its inputs; the poster is blocked, but the room booking can run now.

question: You ask Sam to format a report but have not sent him the file yet. When can Sam start?
why: Delegation includes the handoff; Sam's task has no input until the file arrives.

claim.text: Delegation includes the handoff; Sam's task has no input until the file arrives.

question: Order X gives less total waiting. Order Y misses no deadline. Which order is better?
why: Waiting and lateness measure different things; 'better' needs an objective chosen first.

claim.text: Waiting and lateness measure different things; 'better' needs an objective chosen first.

question: You filter by type = spreadsheet and owner = Lee. Which file matches?
why: Combined filters keep only files that match both conditions: a spreadsheet owned by Lee.

claim.text: Combined filters keep only files that match both conditions: a spreadsheet owned by Lee.

question: You search for "red car" in quotes. Which message matches?
why: Quotes require the words next to each other in that order; only 'red car' as a sequence matches.

claim.text: Quotes require the words next to each other in that order; only 'red car' as a sequence matches.

question: You want messages about 'budget' but not the weekly digest. Which Gmail search fits?
why: The minus sign excludes messages containing 'digest'; OR adds them, and 'budget digest' requires both words.

claim.text: The minus sign excludes messages containing 'digest'; OR adds them, and 'budget digest' requires both words.

question: Yesterday you edited a spreadsheet you created in 2019. Which filter finds it as yesterday's work?
why: Editing updates the modified date; the created date stays in 2019.

claim.text: Editing updates the modified date; the created date stays in 2019.

question: Which naming makes the 10 March 2025 file sort before the 5 January 2026 file alphabetically?
why: Year-first names put the largest unit first; '05-01-2026' and 'Jan' sort ahead of 2025 as text.

claim.text: Year-first names put the largest unit first; '05-01-2026' and 'Jan' sort ahead of 2025 as text.

question: A plain text sort lists draft1, draft10, draft2. Which names sort as 1, 2, 10?
why: Text sort compares character by character, so '10' comes before '2'; padding to equal width fixes it.

claim.text: Text sort compares character by character, so '10' comes before '2'; padding to equal width fixes it.

question: You email three attachments from three projects, each named budget.xlsx. Which naming keeps them distinguishable?
why: The folder does not travel with the attachment; a project prefix in the name does.

claim.text: The folder does not travel with the attachment; a project prefix in the name does.

question: Two files both display as 'invoice'. What tells you which one is the PDF?
options: The date it was last modified
why: The base names match; the extension is the field that differs by format, though it does not verify the contents.

claim.text: The base names match; the extension is the field that differs by format, though it does not verify the contents.

question: A recipe is tagged 'dinner' and 'vegan'. You fix a typo after opening it from 'vegan'. What do you see when you open it from 'dinner'?
why: Both tags point to one document, so there is only one copy to edit.

claim.text: Both tags point to one document, so there is only one copy to edit.

question: Two files are both named photo.jpg. How do you check whether they are duplicates?
why: Names can collide; only matching contents show a duplicate.

claim.text: Names can collide; only matching contents show a duplicate.

question: Path A is home/work/2024/old/report. Path B is home/work/report. How many fewer folders do you open to reach B?
why: A passes through four folders and B through two; removing '2024' and 'old' saves two levels.

claim.text: A passes through four folders and B through two; removing '2024' and 'old' saves two levels.

question: You want the last file you worked on. Which sort puts it on top?
why: Size and name do not record when a file changed; sort by the field that answers the question.

claim.text: Size and name do not record when a file changed; sort by the field that answers the question.

question: A search for 'lease' finds nothing, but you are sure the file existed last week. What should you widen?
why: Active-only search leaves trashed files out; including that state can reveal it, within the product's retention rules.

claim.text: Active-only search leaves trashed files out; including that state can reveal it, within the product's retention rules.

question: You remember a document mentions 'invoice 4471' but not its title. Which search can find it?
options: Sort all titles from A to Z
why: The number is in the body; a title-only search never looks there.

claim.text: The number is in the body; a title-only search never looks there.

question: 5 messages are from Ana, 8 have attachments, and 2 are both. How many messages match 'from Ana OR has an attachment'?
why: OR counts the union: 5 + 8 − 2 shared = 11. AND would keep only the 2.

claim.text: OR counts the union: 5 + 8 − 2 shared = 11. AND would keep only the 2.

question: Which handoff line settles who does what next?
why: It names an owner, an action and an object; one line lacks the owner, the other the object.

claim.text: It names an owner, an action and an object; one line lacks the owner, the other the object.

question: Which message asks for a decision someone can settle in one reply?
options: 'Venue: Hall A or Hall B? Reply by Friday'
'Let me know about the venue sometime'
why: Named alternatives and a reply time bound the decision; open prompts can mean almost anything.

claim.text: Named alternatives and a reply time bound the decision; open prompts can mean almost anything.

question: Your team works in London and Tokyo. Which deadline means the same moment for both?
why: A date, a clock time and a time zone fix one moment; 'end of day' and bare times depend on where you read them.

claim.text: A date, a clock time and a time zone fix one moment; 'end of day' and bare times depend on where you read them.

question: Which agenda item says what the meeting must produce?
options: 'Budget: Ravi picks option A or B'
why: It names the outcome (a choice) and who decides; the others name only a topic.

claim.text: It names the outcome (a choice) and who decides; the others name only a topic.

question: Six months later someone asks why the team picked supplier B. Which record answers them?
options: 'Chose B after a long, careful discussion'
'Chose B: only one able to deliver by June'
why: Only the record with the reason lets a later reader inspect the decision; who and when do not say why.

claim.text: Only the record with the reason lets a later reader inspect the decision; who and when do not say why.

question: You hand a half-done report to a colleague. Which note lets them restart without asking?
why: Artifact, last completed step and next check give a restart point; 'nearly finished' gives none.

claim.text: Artifact, last completed step and next check give a restart point; 'nearly finished' gives none.

question: Which bug report lets someone try to reproduce the problem?
why: Input, expected and actual output let someone rerun the same case; a symptom alone does not.

claim.text: Input, expected and actual output let someone rerun the same case; a symptom alone does not.

question: There are three drafts of the proposal. Which request points at one review target?
why: Version and scope name exactly what to review; 'the latest' depends on which drafts each reader has.

claim.text: Version and scope name exactly what to review; 'the latest' depends on which drafts each reader has.

question: Which status update tells your manager what is stopping progress?
options: 'Draft done; blocked on sales data; asking Bo'
'Worked on the report all day today'
'Report going well; very busy this week'
why: It separates what is done, the blocker and the next action; activity alone names no obstacle.

claim.text: It separates what is done, the blocker and the next action; activity alone names no obstacle.

question: An email has three links. Which link text tells you where it goes before you click?
why: A label that names the artifact, version and section states the destination; 'click here' does not.

claim.text: A label that names the artifact, version and section states the destination; 'click here' does not.

question: You copy paragraph 2 and paste it at the end. How many instances of paragraph 2 does the document now have?
why: Copy leaves the source in place and adds an instance at the destination.

claim.text: Copy leaves the source in place and adds an instance at the destination.

question: In 'A B C D' you cut B and paste it after D. What is the result?
why: Cut removes B from its place; pasting puts it after D.

claim.text: Cut removes B from its place; pasting puts it after D.

question: A word reads 'cat'. In one edit you change it to 'dog', then press Undo, then Redo. What does it read?
why: Undo steps back to 'cat'; Redo reapplies the change to 'dog'.

claim.text: Undo steps back to 'cat'; Redo reapplies the change to 'dog'.

question: Text: 'cat, cat, cat'. You select the second 'cat' and type 'dog'. What is the result?
why: Typing over a selection replaces only that position; replace-all would change every match.

claim.text: Typing over a selection replaces only that position; replace-all would change every match.

question: You search for 'tax' and press Find next three times. What has changed in the document's text?
why: Find moves the highlight between matches; the stored text is unchanged.

claim.text: Find moves the highlight between matches; the stored text is unchanged.

question: You paste a bold red heading with 'paste as plain text'. What arrives?
options: The words, still bold and red
Only the bold and red styling
The words, without bold or red
why: Plain-text paste keeps the words and drops the source styling; exact paste options vary by app.

claim.text: Plain-text paste keeps the words and drops the source styling; exact paste options vary by app.

question: You plan to replace every 'Dr' with 'Drive' in an address list. What should you check in the preview first?
why: A preview shows the full scope of a replace-all, including matches you did not mean, like the title in 'Dr Smith'.

claim.text: A preview shows the full scope of a replace-all, including matches you did not mean, like the title in 'Dr Smith'.

question: You want to try a risky reformat of a spreadsheet but may want the old version back. What do you do first?
options: Duplicate it and edit the copy
Rename it, then edit the file
Edit it, then press Save at once
why: A duplicate keeps the original beside the edited version; renaming or saving still changes the one file.

claim.text: A duplicate keeps the original beside the edited version; renaming or saving still changes the one file.

question: You zoom a document to 200%. What happens to its word count?
options: It doubles as the letters grow
It drops as fewer words fit
why: Zoom changes the view, not the stored text.

claim.text: Zoom changes the view, not the stored text.

question: A is selected in the left panel. You click into the right panel, which holds B, without selecting anything. In this lesson's model, what decides a command's target?
why: Focus and selection are separate state; the target is the selected item. Real apps differ in how focus and shortcuts behave.

claim.text: Focus and selection are separate state; the target is the selected item. Real apps differ in how focus and shortcuts behave.
